blocks.text: Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd (HAL) designs, develops, manufactures, upgrades, repairs and overhauls aircraft, helicopters, aero-engines, avionics, accessories and aerospace structures, principally for the Indian armed forces [F] (SCREENER). It is a Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise in which the President of India, acting through the Ministry of Defence, holds 71.64% [F] (AR2026 p.104). Operations are organised into five complexes - Bangalore, MiG, Helicopter, Accessories and Design - comprising 20 production divisions and 10 R&D centres at ten geographic locations across seven states [F] (AR2026 p.88). The Business Responsibility report puts the physical footprint at 30 plants and five offices in India plus three offices abroad [F] (AR2026 p.117).

**The business is not primarily a manufacturer; it is a services business with a manufacturing arm.** In FY26, repair, maintenance and overhaul of aircraft, helicopters and engines contributed 65% of turnover and manufacture of aircraft and helicopters 30% [F] (AR2026 p.117). On the FY26 earnings call management put manufacturing revenue at Rs 9,227 cr and 'ROH revenue' (which on its definition includes spares) at Rs 20,524 cr against total revenue from operations of Rs 33,050 cr [MC] (CALL May 2026). The audited revenue note gives the same manufacturing figure exactly - inland sale of finished goods Rs 9,227 cr - alongside inland repair and overhaul services of Rs 15,619 cr and inland spares of Rs 4,905 cr [F] (AR2026 p.226).

blocks.caption: Revenue composition, FY26 (standalone, as disclosed)

blocks.text: Geography is close to a single country. India accounted for Rs 31,290 cr and all export markets Rs 501 cr in FY26, or 1.58% of turnover [F] (AR2026 p.232, p.117). Customers are close to a single buyer: the notes state that around 98% of turnover, around 99% of trade receivables and contract assets, around 98% of claims receivable and around 100% of customer advances relate to Government and Government-related entities [F] (AR2026 p.248). The primary customers named are the Indian Air Force, Indian Navy, Indian Army and Indian Coast Guard [F] (AR2026 p.117).

How HAL is paid matters more than what it sells. Gross advances from defence customers stood at Rs 73,009 cr at 31 March 2026 against Rs 51,288 cr a year earlier [F] (AR2026 p.284). The customer funds the working capital; HAL earns interest on the float. That is the engine of both the cash flow and the other income.

subsections.title: Listing status and the evidence base

blocks.text: HAL is not a recent listing. The Government divested 10.03% in FY2017-18 and the shares listed on 28 March 2018 [F] (AR2026 p.25). Subsequent offers for sale in August 2020 (15%) and March 2023 (3.5%) took Government holding from 89.97% to 75.15% and then to 71.64% after an employee tranche in April 2023 [F] (AR2026 p.24-25). One equity share of Rs 10 was sub-divided into two of Rs 5 with record date 29 September 2023 [F] (AR2026 p.24). Eight years of listed disclosure and ten years of statements are therefore available [F] (NUMBERS).

items: **The evidence base for this quarter is thin in one specific and important way: there is no earnings call for the June 2026 quarter in the record.** The latest transcript available is the Q4 FY26 call of 15 May 2026 [F] (CALL May 2026). All Q1 FY27 statements in this report come from the statements data, not from management commentary [F] (NUMBERS).

Management holds an annual, not quarterly, analyst call. Transcripts exist for May 2023, May 2024, May 2025 and May 2026 only. On the May 2024 call the then CFO acknowledged the gap - 'as somebody was pointing out we would also be happy to have this analyst call at least once in a quarter' - and the cadence has not changed since [MC] (CALL May 2024). [AI] Investors are therefore blind between May prints.

The most recent investor presentation in the record is May 2023 [F] (PPT May 2023). There is no FY26 investor deck in evidence; the order-book split table that the 2023 deck provided has no current equivalent. [AI] Disclosure quality has gone backwards on this dimension.

**No operating-segment disclosure exists at all.** Government companies engaged in defence production are exempted from Ind AS 108, and HAL uses the exemption in full: Clause 37 of Note 49 contains the exemption text and nothing else [F] (AR2026 p.255). Neither segment revenue nor segment profit is published.

The credit rating opinion is prepared on a standalone analytical approach and its FY25 figures (TOI Rs 30,146 cr, PBILDT Rs 8,801 cr, PAT Rs 8,317 cr) differ from the consolidated statements data (sales Rs 30,981 cr, EBITDA Rs 9,621 cr, PAT Rs 8,364 cr) [F] (RATING); [F] (NUMBERS). The two are on different bases and are not reconciled in either document.

blocks.text: Classification of drivers: **structural** - items 1, 3 and 8 (monopoly by construction, the overhaul annuity, and the advance-funded model as long as the order cycle persists); **company-specific** - items 5, 6 and 7 (LCA execution, the capacity already installed, diversification optionality); **cyclical** - items 2 and 4, which are functions of the current Indian defence capital-outlay cycle and the interest-rate environment on a Rs 46,192 cr cash balance, and which reverse if order inflow slows [AI].

subsections.title: Bear thesis - the strongest reasons not to own it

items: **1. The price implies growth that nothing in the evidence supports.** The reverse DCF says today's enterprise value requires about 62.5% annual sales growth for five years, against a base-case equivalent of 8.6% [F] (NUMBERS). Reported nine-year sales growth is 7.0%, five-year 7.8% and three-year 7.1% [F] (NUMBERS). Even the bull DCF, at 12.6% starting growth fading to 13.0% and a 33% EBITDA margin, values the equity at Rs 1,265.1 per share against a market price of Rs 4,905 [F] (NUMBERS).

**2. Execution, not demand, is the binding constraint, and it has failed for three consecutive years.** The LCA Mk1A contract required 3 aircraft in FY24, 16 in FY25 and 16 in FY26 - 35 in total. As at the date of the FY26 accounts, not one had been issued a Signalling Out Certificate [F] (AR2026 p.251). Liquidated damages have been provided for all 35 [F] (AR2026 p.251). In May 2024 management said 16 would be delivered in FY25 [MC] (CALL May 2024); in May 2025 it said GE had committed 12 engines and 12 aircraft would be ready [MC] (CALL May 2025); in May 2026 it said 20 [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**3. Reported profit growth in FY26 came mostly from lower provisioning and higher interest income, not from the operating business.** PBT rose Rs 1,292 cr year on year [F] (AR2026 p.182). Within that, the provisions charge fell Rs 1,225 cr (Rs 2,530 cr to Rs 1,305 cr) and other income rose Rs 1,138 cr [F] (AR2026 p.182); [F] (AR2026 p.226). [AI] Strip both out and the operating business went backwards.

**4. Other income is now 30.8% of profit before tax, the highest in the ten-year record [F] (NUMBERS).** Interest income of Rs 3,087 cr in FY26 is earned on a customer-funded cash pile [F] (AR2026 p.226). It is not a franchise return; it is a float return, and it reverses when advances are consumed.

**5. Revenue includes provision write-backs.** 'Provisions no longer required' of Rs 1,155 cr in FY26 (Rs 835 cr in FY25) are recognised inside Revenue from Operations, not below the line [F] (AR2026 p.227). That is 3.5% of reported revenue from operations and 3.6% of turnover [E].

**6. Working capital has deteriorated sharply and inventory is now the balance sheet.** Inventory days went from 544 in FY24 to 736 in FY25 to 859 in FY26; working-capital days from 37 to 121 to 301 [F] (NUMBERS). Work-in-progress alone rose from Rs 7,889 cr (opening FY25) to Rs 15,540 cr to Rs 25,569 cr [F] (AR2026 p.228). The company's own inventory turnover ratio fell from 1.73x to 1.21x [F] (AR2026 p.91).

**7. Import dependence is rising, not falling, which contradicts the indigenisation narrative.** Imported raw materials, spare parts and components were 80% of total consumption in FY26 against 77% in FY25; indigenous content fell from 23% to 20% [F] (AR2026 p.234). CIF imports rose to Rs 19,302 cr from Rs 15,716 cr [F] (AR2026 p.234). MD&A itself lists 'Dependency on foreign OEMs for critical materials and LRUs' as a weakness [F] (AR2026 p.90).

**8. Board composition has been non-compliant for years and the statutory auditor says so.** The sanctioned strength is seven independent directors; at 31 March 2026 five seats including the one woman independent director were vacant [F] (AR2026 p.95). The Company had only one independent director from 28 December 2024 and none from 28 April 2025 [F] (AR2026 p.108). The auditor draws attention to non-compliance with Regulation 17(1) and Section 149(4), and to the Audit Committee, NRC, SRC and RMC not being validly constituted until 1 June 2025 [F] (AR2026 p.157). Stock exchanges imposed fines [F] (AR2026 p.108). One of the two independent directors appointed in May 2025, Dr S.D. Premkumar, resigned on 5 April 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.280).

**9. Pricing power is weaker than the monopoly implies.** Prices are set through a Pricing Policy Review Committee mechanism with a single customer that knows HAL's cost base. The Fixed Price Quotation arising from the 3rd PPRC runs only to FY23; the 4th PPRC is still in progress, so FY24, FY25 and FY26 prices are not firmed up and sales have been recognised provisionally, with FY26 taken at FY25 prices without escalation [F] (AR2026 p.249-250). [AI] Three years of unsettled pricing on a material part of the book is an open revenue-measurement risk in both directions.

**10. The float can reverse.** CFO of Rs 10,906 cr in FY26 was produced despite an Rs 9,180 cr inventory build, an Rs 2,804 cr receivable and contract-asset build and an Rs 5,485 cr build in other assets, because financial liabilities, provisions and other liabilities rose Rs 20,341 cr [F] (AR2026 p.324). [AI] If order inflow slows, the advance inflow stops while the inventory unwind still has to be financed.

subsections.title: Key debates: what the market may be getting wrong, in both directions

blocks.caption: Live debates

The backlog is real and contracted [F] (AR2026 p.35), but it converted at 7% revenue growth in FY26 and 2% in FY25 [F] (NUMBERS), and management guides 10-12% for FY27 [MC] (CALL May 2026). CARE says manufacturing orders of Rs 2,24,486 cr are 'to be executed in the next 7-8 years' [F] (RATING)

Is the working-capital blow-out a red flag?
Working-capital days of 301 signal deteriorating discipline

The build is customer-funded: gross defence advances rose Rs 21,721 cr in FY26 to Rs 73,009 cr [F] (AR2026 p.284) while inventory rose Rs 9,180 cr [F] (AR2026 p.324). CARE notes 'significant amount of interest-free advances outstanding for the orders under execution' and nil utilisation of working-capital limits [F] (RATING)
Bullish - the headline ratio overstates the problem, though the inventory itself is real and undelivered
Strip out the Rs 3,743 cr of other income and the business is much smaller

Both parts are true. Other income is 30.8% of PBT [F] (NUMBERS), but it is the return on a float the customer supplies interest-free and which is contractually tied to the order book. [AI] It is durable while the order cycle runs and disappears when it does not - which is exactly the definition of cyclical, not of low quality
Neutral - the market is right that it is not franchise profit and wrong that it is transient
Does the DCF's -79% downside mean the stock is worth a fifth of its price?
The model output is the answer

The model applies a 15% WACC and 5.5% terminal growth, computes equity as EV less borrowings, and therefore adds back none of the Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank balances disclosed at 31 March 2026 [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.91). It also excludes the Rs 3,897 cr TTM of other income from the projected cash flows entirely [F] (NUMBERS). [AI] Both choices bias the output down by a material amount that the model does not quantify
Bullish relative to the model - but not enough to close a gap of this size
Is HAL a defence manufacturer or a defence services company?

65% of FY26 turnover was repair and maintenance [F] (AR2026 p.117). Management expects the mix to move to roughly 50:50 over time [MC] (CALL May 2026), and itself notes 'the profitability on repair and overhaul is a little bit higher than manufacturing' [MC] (CALL May 2026)
Bearish on mix - the successful ramp management is selling is a mix shift towards the lower-margin half of the business

blocks.text: [AI] The consensus frame treats HAL as an execution story with a delivery catalyst: the engines arrive, 20 Tejas are signalled out, manufacturing revenue steps up and the multiple is validated. The evidence supports a different frame. HAL is, today, a cost-plus overhaul annuity attached to a Rs 46,192 cr treasury operation, wrapped around a new-build programme that has missed 35 contracted aircraft deliveries in three years and has provided liquidated damages for every one of them [F] (AR2026 p.251); [F] (AR2026 p.91); [F] (AR2026 p.117). The genuine bull point is not the delivery catalyst but the float: the customer pre-funds Rs 73,009 cr of gross advances, HAL keeps the interest, carries no debt and earns 32% on capital employed [F] (AR2026 p.284); [F] (NUMBERS). The genuine bear point is not the delivery delay but the arithmetic: the reverse DCF requires about 62.5% annual sales growth for five years to justify the price, against a nine-year record of 7.0% [F] (NUMBERS). Whichever of those two facts the market is weighting, it is not weighting both.

subsections.title: What the timeline reveals about how recent the current business is

blocks.text: [AI] The overhaul franchise is old and the manufacturing franchise being sold to investors is new and unproven. HAL has been overhauling Russian and Western fleets for decades - the rating agency notes MRO capability across 'over 17 types of aircrafts/helicopters, which also includes aircrafts not manufactured by HAL' [F] (RATING), and management describes supporting 'aging fleets, some of which are more than 60 years old' [F] (AR2026 p.89). That is the 65% of turnover that works [F] (AR2026 p.117).

[AI] By contrast, almost every programme that justifies the growth narrative has been launched or contracted within the last four years, and none has yet delivered at scale: the 83 LCA Mk1A contract has produced zero signalled-out aircraft [F] (AR2026 p.251); the 97 LCA Mk1A contract was signed in FY26 [MC] (CALL May 2026); the 156 LCH order was signed in FY25 with first delivery contracted for FY27-28 [MC] (CALL May 2026); HTT-40 series production made its maiden sortie in October 2025 [F] (AR2026 p.36); the Su-30MKI upgrade is a design programme expected to run 5-6 years before production begins [MC] (CALL May 2026); LCA Mk2 rollout is targeted for the last quarter of FY27 with certification three years later [MC] (CALL May 2026); [MC] (CALL May 2025). The 12-unit LUH limited series production order, in the pipeline since at least May 2023, had still not been converted into a contract as of the FY26 report, though all helicopters have been produced [F] (AR2026 p.37); [MC] (CALL May 2025).

[AI] Read the timeline as two companies: a seventy-year-old maintenance business generating almost all the cash, and a four-year-old volume-manufacturing start-up generating almost all the expectations.

sections.title: The production and service chain: where value is captured

items: **1. Requirement and Acceptance of Necessity.** The customer (a Service, through the Ministry of Defence) initiates a case; the Defence Acquisition Council accords an Acceptance of Necessity. AoN for the Utility Helicopter-Maritime was accorded 3 April 2023 [F] (AR2026 p.38); AoN for Advanced Light Helicopters was approved 8 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

**2. Costing and contract negotiation.** Cost negotiation committee, then Cabinet Committee on Security approval for large cases. Management on the Su-30 upgrade: 'we are expecting the CCS approval for the current financial year' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] HAL is normally a nominated, not competitive, supplier - MD&A lists as a threat 'Change in preference of regular customers by moving from nomination to competitive procurement' [F] (AR2026 p.89).

**3. Advance and milestone receipt.** The customer pays initial and milestone advances before delivery. Gross advances from defence customers were Rs 73,009 cr at 31 March 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.284). These are interest-free [F] (RATING).

**4. Long-lead procurement.** Purchase orders are placed with foreign and domestic OEMs years ahead. Management: 'as the purchase orders have been placed for 83 LCA long back, our inventories have been purchased' [MC] (CALL May 2026). Imported inputs were 80% of consumption in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.234).

blocks.text: [AI] Value is captured at two points and only two: final integration, because the certification relationship with CEMILAC and the armed forces cannot be bought; and overhaul, because once HAL is the designated overhaul agency the revenue recurs for the platform's service life independently of new orders. Everything between those two points - engines, radar, EW, structures, increasingly even fuselages - is bought in or made by others. That is why imported content is 80% of consumption [F] (AR2026 p.234) and why value added has fallen to 41.5% of value of production in FY26 from 56.7% in FY24 [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.23).

The auditor records the same [F] (AR2026 p.164). **Segment margins are therefore not disclosed for any business line, in any year.** Everything below is either the revenue disaggregation note or management's spoken percentages on the calls.

This is the most important sentence on the FY26 call. The annuity did not grow in real terms. Much development work is internally funded - the IMRH programme carries Rs 4,000 cr of board-sanctioned internal funding and UH-M around Rs 2,000 cr [MC] (CALL May 2024) - which shows up as intangible assets under development, Rs 2,287 cr net at 31 March 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.180), not as revenue

Confirmed [F] (AR2026 p.35). But the export *order* received in FY26 was only Rs 330 cr [F] (AR2026 p.41) and the export order book is 'around INR400 crores' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] The export book is shrinking relative to export sales

subsections.title: Is the export mix change strategy or mix?

blocks.text: [AI] It is neither - it is noise. The Rs 101 cr increase in export sales in FY26 is 0.3% of turnover and is largely two Hindustan-228 aircraft delivered to JAGS Aviation, Guyana within two months of contract signature [F] (AR2026 p.37). The export strategy is genuine in intent - new channel partners appointed in Africa, the Middle East and South East Asia, participation at airshows in Paris, Dubai, Algeria and Malaysia, and a stated strategy of 'Opening Export Offices in the target geographies' [F] (AR2026 p.41); [F] (AR2026 p.89) - but it has produced no order of size in four years of documented effort. The pipeline named on the calls (Philippines, Argentina, Egypt, Nigeria, Algeria, Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Botswana, Middle East) has not converted [MC] (CALL May 2023); [MC] (CALL May 2024).

items: **Import exposure is large and growing.** Value of imports on CIF basis was Rs 19,302 cr in FY26 against Rs 15,716 cr in FY25: raw materials Rs 5,381 cr, components and spares Rs 13,810 cr, capital goods Rs 21 cr, special tools Rs 90 cr [F] (AR2026 p.234). Imported inputs were 80% of total consumption [F] (AR2026 p.234).

**Export earnings are trivial by comparison.** FOB exports Rs 430 cr, services Rs 71 cr, income from overseas Rs 113 cr - Rs 614 cr in total [F] (AR2026 p.234). [E] Imports exceed foreign-currency earnings by roughly 31 times.

**The exposure is contractually passed through.** Management: 'as far as the ERV exchange rate, this is already mitigated. It is factored into the contract. So we are not affected' and 'ERV clause is there in each and every contract, and even in the repair and overhaul contracts' [MC] (CALL May 2026). CARE confirms: 'Forex fluctuations are paid on an actual basis by customers' [F] (RATING).

[AI] The pass-through is credible and is the single strongest protection in the model. But note what it implies: if forex and material escalation are reimbursed at actual, HAL's margin is a negotiated spread over a known cost base, not a market price. That is the mechanism by which a monopoly can have weak pricing power. Expenditure in foreign currency on royalty, licence fees, documentation and consultancy rose to Rs 258 cr from Rs 154 cr [F] (AR2026 p.234), with licence fees up nearly four-fold.

**Trade-policy exposure is real and named.** The dominant supply relationships are with a US engine maker (GE F404/F414), a French engine maker (Safran) and Russian OEMs (AL-31FP, RD-33, UAC for SJ-100) [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (AR2026 p.36-37). Management describes a 'geopolitical situation' slowing supplies and has escalated to Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 vendors to diagnose it [MC] (CALL May 2026). In May 2023 it disclosed that 'Certain payments issues were there' with Russian suppliers which 'has been sorted out' [MC] (CALL May 2023).

No tariff rates, duty exposures or trade restrictions are quantified anywhere in the documents. Contingent liabilities for disputed customs duty total roughly Rs 890 cr across many years of appeals [F] (AR2026 p.172), but these are tax disputes, not tariff policy.

**Mitigation:** MoU with MIDHANI on 3 November 2025 to set up a strategic metal bank for critical raw materials 'to mitigate future raw material supply chain issue' [F] (AR2026 p.37); MoU with Yantra India on 23 September 2025 to fund a 10,000-tonne extrusion press [F] (AR2026 p.37); dual-sourcing policy - 'we are trying to identify more than one vendor for the supply of items' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Single-location risk is low by design.** HAL operates 30 plants and five offices in India across ten geographic locations in seven states [F] (AR2026 p.117); [F] (AR2026 p.88). LCA is produced on three lines at two sites (Bangalore and Nashik); helicopters at two (Bangalore and Tumakuru); engines at Koraput and Bangalore [MC] (CALL May 2025); [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Land title risk is disclosed and non-trivial.** The auditor lists immovable properties whose title deeds are not in HAL's name, including approximately 76.5 acres at Bangalore ('Compendium Error ... Few title documents are not available'), 401 acres at Kanpur with no title deed, 282 acres at Korwa, 196 acres of railway siding land at Kasbe Sukena and 69 acres at Ojhar held since 1964 [F] (AR2026 p.167-169). Most carry nil or negligible book value and are covered by the Government Grants Act, 1895 [F] (AR2026 p.168). [AI] Economically minor, but it is an audit-flagged control weakness sixty years old.

sections.title: Customer concentration: is it improving or worsening?

blocks.text: **HAL does not disclose a top-1 / top-5 / top-10 customer table in any year.** What it does disclose is stronger: around 98% of turnover, around 99% of trade receivables and contract assets, around 98% of claims receivable and around 100% of customer advances relate to Government and Government-related entities [F] (AR2026 p.248). The single ultimate counterparty is the Ministry of Defence, which is also the 71.64% promoter [F] (AR2026 p.104).

blocks.caption: Concentration proxies by year, as disclosed
rows: Gross advances from defence customers (Rs cr)

blocks.text: **Is concentration improving or worsening? It is worsening, on every measure that moves.** [AI] The domestic share of sales has risen in each of the last three years as exports failed to keep pace with domestic growth in absolute terms relative to the base; gross advances from defence customers - which are by definition single-counterparty exposure - rose 42% in FY26 to Rs 73,009 cr [F] (AR2026 p.284); and both new-order events of FY26 (97 LCA Mk1A, and the ROH book) were with the same customer [MC] (CALL May 2026). The only genuine diversification in the period is the Pawan Hans order for 10 ALH Dhruv-NG and the Guyana export, together worth an amount not separately disclosed but small enough that non-defence advances fell from Rs 930 cr to Rs 926 cr [F] (AR2026 p.284).

**The counter-argument, which is strong:** concentration risk is normally about credit and bargaining. On credit, the exposure is to the sovereign, receivables are down to 45 days and the auditor's key audit matter notes that HAL makes no impairment provision against government receivables 'based on past experience' [F] (AR2026 p.159); [F] (NUMBERS). On bargaining, the customer pre-pays Rs 73,009 cr interest-free [F] (AR2026 p.284) and reimburses forex and material escalation at actual [F] (RATING). [AI] What remains is not credit risk - it is policy risk: a single decision-maker sets both the volume and the price.

subsections.title: Deep dive 1 - LCA Tejas Mk1A: the programme the price depends on

blocks.text: **Where HAL sits in the value chain.** HAL is the production agency and integrator on a platform jointly designed with the Aeronautical Development Agency. Management is explicit about the split of control: 'LCA, it's a joint production between ADA and HAL' [MC] (CALL May 2026). The engine is GE's; the Uttam AESA radar is DRDO's, with HAL 'only a production agency' that buys from the DCPP partner once DRDO gives production clearance [MC] (CALL May 2026); the fuselage sections come from L&T, VEM, Alpha Tocol and Tata TASL [MC] (CALL May 2025). HAL owns final assembly, equipping, ground run, flight test support and - eventually - the overhaul franchise.

**What actually exists today versus the narrative.** What exists: three production lines (two Bangalore, one Nashik) with a stated installed capacity of 24 aircraft a year [MC] (CALL May 2025); more than 20 airframes built, equipped and engine-ground-run [MC] (CALL May 2026); Rs 8,000-8,100 cr of LCA inventory [MC] (CALL May 2026); and 6 GE engines received [MC] (CALL May 2026). What does not exist: **a single accepted aircraft.** The audited note is unambiguous - 'As on date, no LCA Mk 1A has been issued Signaled out Certificate (SOC)' - against a contractual requirement of 3 in FY24, 16 in FY25 and 16 in FY26, with liquidated damages provided for all 35 [F] (AR2026 p.251).

blocks.text: **Strategic implication [AI].** The inventory-to-revenue conversion, not the order book, is the single measurable variable that decides whether the FY27 guidance holds. Roughly Rs 8,000 cr of LCA inventory converts to roughly Rs 5,000 cr of revenue at the stated per-aircraft realisation across 20 aircraft [E] - about 15% of FY26 turnover. That is what the 10-12% growth guidance is largely made of. subsections.title: Deep dive 2 - Repair and overhaul: the business that actually pays the bills

blocks.text: **Where HAL sits.** HAL is the designated overhaul agency for most of the Indian military fleet, including aircraft it did not build. CARE: 'HAL's MRO capabilities presently include providing services to over 17 types of aircrafts/helicopters, which also includes aircrafts not manufactured by HAL' and HAL 'has a license for providing life-cycle support for platforms such as Su-30, HAWK, Mirage and Jaguar' [F] (RATING). This position is not contestable by a private entrant on any realistic timescale [AI].

**What exists today.** Rs 15,688 cr of ROH services revenue and Rs 4,980 cr of spares in FY26 - 65% of turnover [F] (AR2026 p.226-227); [F] (AR2026 p.117). Installed fleet supported: approximately 340 ALH, 250-plus Su-30MKI, 150 Dorniers, Jaguars with life extended beyond 2035, Su-30 overhaul extending to 2050, and 40 LCA with the first due for overhaul in 2026 [MC] (CALL May 2025). FY23 physical throughput, the last year disclosed at this granularity: 20 Su-30 overhauls, 76 AL-31FP engine overhauls, 30 ALH overhauls, plus roughly Rs 1,000 cr of rotables and roughly Rs 5,000 cr of spares [MC] (CALL May 2023).

**Pricing.** Overhaul is priced through the Pricing Policy Review Committee mechanism, largely cost-plus: 'If it's a full overhaul, we have a separate kind of pricing mechanism, 10 to 15 will be on a cost-plus basis ... there is no fixed percentage that ROH will be a fixed percentage of the equipment cost' [MC] (CALL May 2026). The Fixed Price Quotation from the 3rd PPRC covers only to FY23; FY24 to FY26 sales have been recognised provisionally, FY26 at FY25 prices with no escalation [F] (AR2026 p.249-250).

**The annuity stopped compounding in FY26.** ROH services grew 1.6% and spares fell 13.1% [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.226-227). Management's explanation is structural, not cyclical: 'the repair and overhaul are almost at the same level because we have not added any new platform to our repair and overhaul activities' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] The ROH annuity grows only when new platforms enter service. Zero LCA Mk1A deliveries in three years therefore guarantees no LCA overhaul revenue for at least three years beyond the first delivery - management confirms the lag: 'these LCAs what will be delivering ... maybe like the 3 years, we will come for ROH' [MC] (CALL May 2026). The delivery failure has a second-order cost that nobody is modelling.

blocks.text: The rotary franchise carries a safety record risk that the fighter line does not. Three ALH incidents in 2.5 months in early 2023 [MC] (CALL May 2023) and a Coast Guard accident in January 2025 that grounded the fleet [F] (RATING). Management's 2023 position was that the design was adequate and the fix - replacing aluminium control rods with steel - would cost 'not more than INR200 crores' [MC] (CALL May 2023). Accident rate disclosed at the time: approximately 7.3-7.4 per lakh hours over roughly 3.9 lakh cumulative hours, having risen to around 11 per lakh hour after 2018 from around 9.1-9.2 before [MC] (CALL May 2023). [AI] A further grounding would hit deliveries, overhaul throughput and export prospects simultaneously.

**Strategic implication [AI].** Rotary wing is where the thesis is most likely to be right for the most boring reason: HAL designed the aircraft, owns the certification, built the capacity from cash, has the largest single order in the book, and does not depend on a US engine maker's casting supply. If FY27 disappoints on LCA but the 143-ALH contract lands and LCH deliveries start on schedule in FY28, the growth arithmetic still works. That is the part of the business a sceptic should underwrite; it is also the part that gets the least airtime.

blocks.text: **HAL discloses no capacity utilisation figure, in any year, for any plant or programme.** A search of the annual report returns no installed-capacity schedule and no utilisation percentage. Management's position is that utilisation is full: 'They are not idle because you see production is happening. We have 3 lines now, 2 in Bangalore and 1 in Nashik. Not a single production line is idle ... That is why we were able to do what we showed at the end of March, 21-22 structures ready ... So there's nothing called idle capacity as of now. And we have 97 orders coming. So all these facilities will be 100% utilized throughout the year' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

[AI] That claim is true on an input measure and false on an output measure, and the distinction is the whole argument. On inputs, the lines are running - 21-22 LCA structures built, equipped and engine-ground-run, with roughly Rs 8,000-8,100 cr of LCA inventory to prove it [MC] (CALL May 2026). Work in progress rose from Rs 7,889 cr to Rs 25,569 cr over two years [F] (AR2026 p.228). sections.title: Unit economics: what can and cannot be built

blocks.text: **Direct unit economics cannot be built from HAL's disclosures.** There is no segment reporting [F] (AR2026 p.255), no platform-wise revenue or cost, no production volume schedule in the annual report, and no capacity utilisation figure. What exists is a set of contract values and quantities disclosed on earnings calls, plus two revenue-per-unit statements from the CFO. From these, blended realisation per unit can be estimated. **Material cost and contribution per unit cannot**, because cost of materials is disclosed only in aggregate and against value of production, not against deliveries [F] (AR2026 p.228).

Material intensity has risen 19 percentage points in four years, manpower intensity has drifted up rather than down towards management's stated 16% goal [MC] (CALL May 2024), and value added per employee has now fallen year on year for the first time in the series. Sales per employee keeps rising - which is what management points to - but that is a headcount-denominator effect, not a productivity gain: sales rose 5.6% while headcount fell 2.1% [E].

**What would have to be true for unit economics to improve [AI]:** (i) accepted deliveries would have to rise faster than value of production, converting the Rs 25,569 cr of work-in-progress into revenue and stopping the material-intensity climb; (ii) the 4th PPRC would have to settle FY24-FY26 prices *above* the provisional recognition, since FY26 was booked at FY25 prices with no escalation at all [F] (AR2026 p.250); (iii) indigenous content would have to rise from 20% of consumption, which requires the MIDHANI metal bank and the PTC/Yantra supply chain to actually produce [F] (AR2026 p.234); and (iv) the ROH mix would have to hold rather than dilute to 50:50 as management expects [MC] (CALL May 2026). The FY22-23 anomaly was the settlement of income-tax disputes from 2008 to FY16, generating Rs 2,451 cr of refunds and Rs 830 cr of interest, and management confirmed in May 2023 that 'there is nothing left out now' [MC] (CALL May 2023). [AI] A repeat is not available.

**Depreciation is falling while the gross block rises.** Gross PPE went from Rs 13,475 cr to Rs 14,585 cr in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.180), yet consolidated depreciation fell from Rs 1,785 cr in FY23 to Rs 1,355 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). The FY24 drop was explained as HTT-40 amortisation falling away [MC] (CALL May 2024). Accumulated depreciation of Rs 7,923 cr against gross block of Rs 14,585 cr, plus Rs 501 cr of accumulated impairment, means the asset base is 58% written down [E].
**Interest expense is effectively nil.** Rs 24 cr in FY26 against Rs 5,927 cr of borrowings in FY20; interest cover is 507x [F] (NUMBERS).

**The provisions line is the swing item nobody models.** Rs 2,530 cr charged in FY25, Rs 1,305 cr in FY26 - a Rs 1,225 cr favourable swing against a Rs 1,292 cr increase in PBT [F] (AR2026 p.182). Within that, the Provision for Replacement and Other Charges was Rs 1,264 cr in FY25 (including Rs 843 cr for the crashed Su-30) and Rs 27 cr in FY26, with Rs 613 cr reversed [F] (AR2026 p.281-282). Management's own framing: 'Provision is based on any happening or not happening. So for that reason, last year, that INR800 crores was there, and that INR800 crores is not there in the current year' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Liquidated damages are running at a high level.** LD provision made in FY26 was Rs 722 cr (FY25: Rs 658 cr), with a closing balance of Rs 1,814 cr [F] (AR2026 p.281-282). LD is a key audit matter precisely because 'The liquidated damages recognized being significant in the statement of profit and loss' [F] (AR2026 p.161). [AI] HAL is paying penalties for late delivery at roughly 2.3% of turnover a year and calling the resulting revenue growth 'resilience'.

**Provision write-backs sit inside revenue, not other income.** 'Provisions no Longer Required' of Rs 1,155 cr in FY26 and Rs 835 cr in FY25 are booked as Other Operating Revenue within Revenue from Operations [F] (AR2026 p.227). [AI] This inflates reported revenue growth and the reported operating margin simultaneously.

**The balance sheet has tripled while the fixed assets have not moved.** Total assets went from Rs 51,744 cr in FY17 to Rs 1,34,395 cr in FY26; net fixed assets went from Rs 7,350 cr to Rs 7,293 cr [F] (NUMBERS). 'Other assets' - overwhelmingly inventory, contract assets, cash and bank balances - are Rs 1,21,875 cr, or 90.7% of the balance sheet [E].

**The growth in liabilities is customer money, not borrowed money.** 'Other liabilities' rose from Rs 51,723 cr in FY24 to Rs 93,288 cr in FY26 while borrowings went from Rs 50 cr to Rs 66 cr [F] (NUMBERS). The standalone note identifies the driver precisely: gross advances from defence customers of Rs 73,009 cr against Rs 51,288 cr [F] (AR2026 p.284).

**Equity has compounded without dilution.** Equity capital has been Rs 334 cr since FY18; reserves went from Rs 9,177 cr to Rs 40,707 cr [F] (NUMBERS). No fresh issue, no ESOP - 'The Company has not issued any stock options to its directors' [F] (AR2026 p.102].

**Debt was briefly real and is gone.** Borrowings peaked at Rs 5,927 cr in FY20 (debt/equity 0.45x) and collapsed to Rs 51 cr in FY21 [F] (NUMBERS), coinciding with an extraordinary CFO of Rs 15,263 cr in FY21 and the realisation of government dues noted by the rating agency [F] (RATING).

**Contract assets are large and growing, and a key audit matter.** Rs 19,130 cr at 31 March 2026 against Rs 15,889 cr [F] (AR2026 p.180). Management explains these as delivered-but-unbilled: 'unbilled revenue is against the delivery that has already happened ... because of the documentation and all those things, the non-receipt of documentation we could not bill it' [MC] (CALL May 2026). The provision for doubtful contract assets rose from Rs 214 cr to Rs 357 cr [F] (AR2026 p.282).

**Reserve transfers are formulaic.** Rs 945 cr to the R&D Reserve (15% of operating PAT), Rs 189 cr to the Indigenisation Fund Reserve (3%), Rs 4,886 cr to General Reserve [F] (AR2026 p.35); [F] (AR2026 p.220-221). [AI] These are appropriations, not cash ring-fencing, and do not constrain distributable surplus in practice.

subsections.title: The headline number and why it misleads

blocks.text: Working-capital days stood at 301 at FY26 against a 65-day average, and the rule-based flag in our statements data raises this as an amber item [F] (NUMBERS). The cash conversion cycle was 788 days against 484 days two years earlier [F] (NUMBERS). Taken alone those numbers describe a company losing control of its balance sheet.

**Taken alone, they are wrong.** The metric is computed against trade payables only. HAL's real supplier of working capital is not its vendors - it is its customer. Gross advances from defence customers were Rs 73,009 cr at 31 March 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.284), against inventories of Rs 30,851 cr and contract assets of Rs 19,130 cr [F] (AR2026 p.180). The rating agency makes the same point: 'significant amount of interest-free advances outstanding for the orders under execution have led to negligible reliance of HAL on external borrowings and nil utilisation of its fund-based working capital limits' [F] (RATING).

blocks.text: [AI] Three things move in that table and only one is bad. Debtor days have improved every year and are now the best in the ten-year record at 45 - the rating agency notes receivables have stayed below Rs 4,800 cr on the balance sheet date for four consecutive years [F] (RATING). Payables fell back to 116 days after a 156-day FY25, which is a use of cash. And inventory days rose 315 days in two years, entirely because of work-in-progress: WIP tripled from Rs 7,889 cr (opening FY25) to Rs 25,569 cr [F] (AR2026 p.228).

subsections.title: What drove the change - management's account and the evidence

items: **Management's stated reason, FY25:** 'The inventory holding you may find to be at an increased level from 159 days to 263 days. We believe this is necessary considering the manufacturing cycle times of 18 to 36 months. The work in progress build-up is essential to meet the delivery timelines' [MC] (CALL May 2025).

**Management's stated reason, FY26:** 'we have made up. We don't have only LCA. Many programs are going on ... we built up inventory for repair and overhaul also, spare supply, then we have Su-30, AL-31FP engines, RD-33 engines, then LCH, to some extent, ALH ... HTT-40. LCA is part of it. And as I said, out of 30,000 LCA is around INR8,000 crores' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**The company's own ratio explanation:** 'Inventory Turnover Ratio has reduced during the financial year due to increase in work-in-progress in respect of manufacturing programs viz. LCA MK1A, HTT-40, ALH, LCH, Su-30 and AL-31FP engines etc.' [F] (AR2026 p.92).

**The corroborating evidence is strong and the framing is generous.** Rs 8,000-8,100 cr of the Rs 30,851 cr is LCA [MC] (CALL May 2026). The other Rs 22,800 cr is spread across programmes that are in production. But the reason the WIP has tripled rather than turned is that the acceptances have not happened: zero LCA Mk1A signalled out [F] (AR2026 p.251), all 12 LUH built with no contract [F] (AR2026 p.37), and HTT-40 series deliveries not yet begun [F] (AR2026 p.36). [AI] The inventory build is not primarily a strategic pre-buy. It is the accumulated residue of delivery failure.

**Balances are under reconciliation.** Trade receivables, trade payables, claims receivable, advances, capital advances, deposits and stock lying with sub-contractors 'are under reconciliation', with management stating no material financial impact is expected [F] (AR2026 p.248). Materials with sub-contractors alone were Rs 473 cr [F] (AR2026 p.215). [AI] For a balance sheet of Rs 1.32 lakh crore, a blanket reconciliation caveat across every working-capital line is a notable disclosure.

subsections.title: Cash-conversion consequence, covenants and bank limits

items: **Consequence to date: none, because the customer funds it.** CFO of Rs 10,906 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS); nil borrowings; nil utilisation of sanctioned fund-based working-capital limits of Rs 4,000 cr for the twelve months to 31 October 2025 [F] (RATING); free cash and cash equivalents of Rs 43,465 cr at 30 September 2025 [F] (RATING) rising to Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank balances at 31 March 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.91).

**Facilities and ratings:** CARE AAA/Stable for long-term and A1+ for short-term on Rs 6,050 cr of fund-based and non-fund-based facilities, reaffirmed 9 March 2026 [F] (RATING). The annual report describes the same as CARE AAA/Stable for short-term credit facilities of Rs 4,000 cr and A1+ for non-fund-based limits of Rs 2,050 cr, with identical ratings from ICRA [F] (AR2026 p.109).

**No financial covenants are disclosed.** CARO reports no default and no term loans [F] (AR2026 p.173). The rating agency's negative triggers function as de facto covenants: a significant fall in the order book or dilution of Government stake below majority; total debt to PBILDT exceeding 0.50x on a sustained basis; or a significant decline in surplus liquidity [F] (RATING).

**Quarterly stock statements agree with the books** - CARO confirms this explicitly for working-capital limits in excess of Rs 5 cr [F] (AR2026 p.170). [AI] That removes one common forensic concern outright.

[AI] **The risk is not liquidity today; it is the asymmetry of the unwind.** Advances arrive when orders are signed and are consumed when aircraft are delivered. FY25 and FY26 were both years of exceptional order inflow (Rs 1,25,280 cr and Rs 97,028 cr) and near-zero fighter deliveries, so advances built and inventory built together. The reverse configuration - a year with low order inflow and high deliveries - has not been tested under the current balance sheet. In that year, operating cash flow would fall sharply even as reported profit rose.

HAL also leases an Avro aircraft **from** the Indian Air Force at Rs 3.22 cr per year [F] (AR2026 p.235).

**The pending Su-30 replacement claim is a real liability that sits in provisions, not contingents.** Rs 843 cr was provided in FY25 because 'Customer is also demanding for the replacement of equivalent Aircraft. As there is no replacement aircraft (Cat-B) available' [F] (AR2026 p.249). The insurance recovery of Rs 141 cr was received in January 2025 [F] (AR2026 p.249). [AI] The net exposure of roughly Rs 700 cr has been taken; the outcome is still open.

**The GE penalty is an undisclosed asset, not a liability.** Asked about penalties on GE for engine delays, the CMD said terms exist in the purchase order but 'It's in the contract, so that's why we don't want to give any' number, and management added 'we cannot quantify them right now. Let the delivery happen, then we'll see' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] Any recovery would be an unmodelled positive; no contingent asset is recognised.

blocks.text: **On solvency and liquidity, the balance sheet is close to unimpeachable.** Nil debt across the full year, Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank, AAA/A1+ from two agencies, nil guarantees, no goodwill, contingent liabilities that are overwhelmingly reimbursable by the customer, and independently verified agreement between stock statements and books [F] (AR2026 p.36, p.91, p.109, p.233); [F] (AR2026 p.170); [F] (RATING).

**On asset realisation, one question dominates everything else.** Rs 30,851 cr of inventory (83% work-in-progress) and Rs 19,130 cr of contract assets together are Rs 49,981 cr, or 122% of shareholders' equity [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.180-181). Work-in-progress is physically verified only once a year and the key audit matter records that 'the verification of WIP is done on annual basis' [F] (AR2026 p.160). The redundancy provision against work-in-progress has been frozen at Rs 266 cr for two years while WIP itself rose Rs 10,030 cr [F] (AR2026 p.214). [AI] That is the one line in the accounts where a forensic investor should want more, and the annual physical-verification cadence on a Rs 25,569 cr balance is not commensurate with its size.

There is no second Indian company that can integrate and certify a fighter airframe, and the barrier is not capital but decades of type certification, flight-test infrastructure and an airworthiness relationship with CEMILAC and the Services. That position is durable. But it confers far less pricing power than the word 'monopoly' implies, because the counterparty on the other side is a single buyer that knows HAL's cost base in detail, prices through a cost-plus committee mechanism, and has explicitly retained the option to move from nomination to tender [F] (AR2026 p.89); [MC] (CALL May 2026).

[AI] The private sector is not competing with HAL - it is being deliberately built into HAL's supply chain by HAL itself. L&T, Tata TASL, VEM, Alpha Tocol and PTC supply the structures and castings that HAL used to make in-house, which is exactly why value added has fallen from 56.7% to 41.5% of value of production in two years [E]. That trade - outsourcing volume to free integration capacity - is rational and is management's stated strategy ('so that I will be the core integrator') [MC] (CALL May 2026). It also progressively narrows HAL to the two activities where it is irreplaceable, and progressively teaches the private sector the rest. The competitive threat is not a rival bidding against HAL today; it is the supply chain HAL is training being able to bid against it in a decade.

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **1. Does a moat that cannot be converted into price count as a moat?** Every measure of protection here - certification, switching costs, relationship - protects HAL's *volume*, not its *margin*. Price is set through the PPRC on a cost-plus basis with escalation and forex reimbursed at actual [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (RATING), and the 4th PPRC has not settled FY24, FY25 or FY26 prices at all, with FY26 recognised at FY25 prices with no escalation [F] (AR2026 p.250). A business that cannot raise price above cost has a franchise in revenue and none in return. The 30% operating margin exists by administrative decision, not by market power. **Nothing in the documents tells us what would happen to that margin if the buyer decided it should be 20%.**

**2. Would the moat survive a change in procurement policy?** HAL's own MD&A lists as a threat 'Change in preference of regular customers by moving from nomination to competitive procurement' and 'Mainly dependent on MoD for the contracts. Any change in procurement policy / preference can adversely affect our ability to grow or maintain our sales, earnings and cash flow' [F] (AR2026 p.89). The AMCA tender is an early test - HAL is a hopeful participant in a D&D competition, not the designated producer [MC] (CALL May 2026). The moat scorecard measures technical and relational barriers. It cannot measure a policy decision, and a policy decision is the only thing that could remove the moat in a single step.

blocks.text: [AI] **HAL has one of the most secure competitive positions available in Indian industry and one of the least commercially valuable forms of it.** The overhaul franchise scores 9-10 on switching costs, regulatory barriers and relationship durability, and should be underwritten as a multi-decade annuity: once HAL is the designated overhaul agency for a fleet, the revenue recurs for the platform's whole service life independently of any new order win. That is the defensible core, it is 65% of turnover, and it is the higher-margin half on management's own account [F] (AR2026 p.117); [MC] (CALL May 2026).

[AI] The two scores of 2 - network effects and input control - are where the risk lives, and input control is the one that has already cost shareholders three years of fighter revenue. A monopoly integrator that imports 80% of its inputs and does not own the engine, the radar or the electronic-warfare suite of its flagship programme is not in control of its own delivery schedule. The moat protects HAL from competitors. It does not protect it from GE, from DRDO's certification queue, or from the Ministry that owns it.

CARE's weakness section says so directly [F] (RATING).

**'HAL is a drone and UCAV play.'** CATS Warrior flight test is only *planned* for FY27; the RUAV is in ground test; HAL has explicitly refused the volume drone market on price grounds [F] (AR2026 p.38); [MC] (CALL May 2026); [MC] (CALL May 2025). **'HAL is a civil MRO play.'** Certification was still in process as at May 2025 and no civil MRO revenue appears in the FY26 accounts [MC] (CALL May 2025).

**'The order book converts to double-digit growth.'** The backlog executed over HAL's own stated 7-8 year horizon implies Rs 31,817-36,363 cr of annual revenue against FY26 turnover of Rs 31,792 cr [E]. Revenue grew 6.8% in FY26 and 2.0% in FY25 [F] (NUMBERS).

**'Manufacturing mix shift is margin-accretive.'** Management concedes overhaul is the more profitable activity and simultaneously guides an unchanged 30-31% margin as mix moves from 30:70 towards 50:50 [MC] (CALL May 2026). The two claims are not reconciled anywhere.

blocks.text: [AI] Strip out the unsupported themes and what remains is a genuinely good, genuinely slow business: a certified monopoly overhaul franchise on an ageing and expanding fleet, 65% of revenue, higher-margin, growing at low single digits; attached to an integration business with an eight-year backlog that it has not been able to execute; funded entirely by a customer that is also the owner; generating a Rs 46,192 cr float on which the interest is now 31% of pre-tax profit. Every one of those five clauses is audited. None of them is a growth story.

[AI] The structural themes that could change the picture - exports, unmanned systems, space, civil MRO, global supply chain - are collectively worth approximately Rs 501 cr of disclosed revenue and approximately Rs 400 cr of disclosed order book today [F] (AR2026 p.35); [MC] (CALL May 2026). blocks.text: **The pattern is precise and it has held for four consecutive years: HAL's management is reliable on what it can negotiate and unreliable on what it must deliver.** Every order-book and order-inflow guidance has been met or beaten. Every physical delivery guidance - LCA Mk1A, HTT-40, LUH, LCA Mk2 first flight, export breakthrough - has been missed. Revenue guidance has been missed in two of the last three years. Capex has run a third below the announced plan and the plan has now been cut.

items: **The guidance is restated rather than reconciled.** The FY25 promise of 'consistent double-digit growth' [MC] (CALL May 2024) became a delivered 2.0%, and the FY26 call did not revisit the earlier promise - it simply issued a new one [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] No management statement in the four transcripts acknowledges a prior guidance miss in those terms.

**Guidance is conditional in ways that are easy to miss.** The FY27 10-12% figure is explicitly contingent: 'we are confident that LCA and HTT-40 will be delivered, and whatever guidance we are giving, 10% to 12%, we'll be able to maintain it' [MC] (CALL May 2026). Management also refers to 'our ways and means to see that if something goes wrong ... we will always have our plan B in the year that we cannot tell you right now' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] Given that provision write-backs contributed Rs 1,155 cr to FY26 revenue [F] (AR2026 p.227), an investor is entitled to ask what 'plan B' consists of.

**Engine-supply commitments from the supplier have been passed through verbatim without discount.** GE 'promised a supply of 12 engines in this calendar year ... This is confirmed, and they will be sticking to this schedule' [MC] (CALL May 2025); six arrived [MC] (CALL May 2026). The FY27 version - 'GE is committing another 20 engines - 15 to 20, he is telling, but not the exact number. So we are expecting around 20' - is a looser commitment presented with equal confidence [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**One genuine improvement in candour.** The FY26 call contains the clearest negative disclosure in four years: 'the repair and overhaul are almost at the same level because we have not added any new platform' [MC] (CALL May 2026). [AI] That is management volunteering a structural limitation rather than being drawn to it, and it deserves credit.

[AI] **How to use the guidance going forward:** treat order inflow guidance as reliable and directionally conservative; treat delivery and revenue guidance as an upper bound requiring independent confirmation from engine receipts and Signalling Out Certificates; and treat margin guidance as a statement about the *definition* of margin rather than about operating performance, since HAL's own published operating margin fell in the year that management said 30-31% was being maintained.

blocks.text: On the surface this is a strong earnings-quality record and the rule-based screen flags it green: 'Operating cash flow was 1.31x reported profit over the last three years' [F] (NUMBERS). Every year since FY21 has converted profit into cash at or above 1.0x, and free cash flow was Rs 26,804 cr over three years and Rs 42,534 cr over five [F] (NUMBERS).

**Under the surface, the conversion is not coming from profit.** In FY26, operating cash flow of Rs 10,906 cr was achieved despite Rs 18,143 cr absorbed by inventories, receivables and other assets, because financial liabilities, provisions and other liabilities rose Rs 20,341 cr - overwhelmingly customer advances and milestone receipts [F] (AR2026 p.324); [F] (AR2026 p.284). [AI] HAL's CFO/PAT ratio is a measure of its order-inflow rate, not of its accrual discipline. blocks.text: [AI] **Earnings quality is adequate rather than high, and it is more fragile than the CFO/PAT ratio suggests.** There is no aggressive capitalisation, no dilution, no receivables problem, no goodwill and no debt. All forward figures in this report come from our discounted cash flow model and no others are produced. **Capex tied to growth** through the fixed-asset-turnover rule, which on this growth profile implies capex broadly in line with the Rs 2,000-3,000 cr per annum the rating agency expects [F] (RATING).

items: **Sales** = accepted deliveries x realisation + overhaul and spares + development. Accepted deliveries depend on (a) GE engine receipts, guided at 15-20 in FY27 from August 2026, with a 30-45 day fit-out lag [MC] (CALL May 2026); (b) closure of LCA Mk1A certification 'refinements' [MC] (CALL May 2026); (c) Honeywell engine flow for HTT-40 [MC] (CALL May 2026); and (d) no repeat of a fleet grounding [F] (RATING).

**Overhaul and spares** = installed fleet x overhaul cycle x PPRC-determined price. Grows only when new platforms enter service - management is explicit that FY26 was flat 'because we have not added any new platform' [MC] (CALL May 2026), and the LCA overhaul cycle starts roughly three years after first delivery [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**EBITDA margin** = mix (overhaul is the higher-margin half) x PPRC price settlement x material intensity x the provisions charge. The 4th PPRC has not settled FY24, FY25 or FY26 prices; FY26 was booked at FY25 prices with no escalation [F] (AR2026 p.250).
**FCFF** = EBITDA - cash tax - capex - change in working capital. The working-capital term is the swing factor: the model assumes 153 days against an actual 301 in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS).
**Terminal value** = year-5 FCFF grown at 5.5% and capitalised at 15% less 5.5%. Two-thirds of the answer sits here.

subsections.title: What the forecast deliberately does not assume

items: **It does not model the order book.** Rs 2,54,538 cr of backlog enters only through the growth rate [F] (AR2026 p.35). No conversion schedule, no LCA delivery ramp and no LCH production start from FY28 is built in.

**It does not model other income.** Rs 3,897 cr of trailing other income and Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank balances are excluded from cash flows and from equity value entirely [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.91).

**It does not model the customer-advance float.** The Rs 73,009 cr of gross defence advances that fund the working capital are captured only as a 153-day working-capital assumption [F] (AR2026 p.284).
**It does not model a PPRC settlement in either direction.** Three years of provisional pricing could settle above or below the recognised amounts [F] (AR2026 p.250).
**It does not model liquidated damages, provision write-backs or offset credits** - the items that have moved reported profit most in each of the last three years [F] (AR2026 p.182, p.227, p.159).
**It does not model exports, unmanned systems, space, civil MRO or the Safran LEAP programme.** Together these are approximately 1.6% of turnover today [F] (AR2026 p.117).
**It does not model a change in procurement policy, a fleet grounding, a further engine slip, or a Government stake sale** - the four events most likely to move the answer discontinuously.

[AI] Taken together, the omissions are not symmetric: the excluded cash and other income argue for a higher value, while the excluded execution risk argues for a lower one. **The model is best read as a valuation of the operating business only, at a demanding discount rate, ignoring the treasury.**

subsections.title: Interpreting the DCF and its assumptions

items: **The model is meaningful on its own terms.** It is flagged as available and meaningful in the statements data, uses a growth rate derived from HAL's realised record, a margin consistent with management guidance, and a capex rule anchored to the company's own fixed-asset turnover [F] (NUMBERS).

**Its central weakness is the treatment of the balance sheet.** Equity value equals enterprise value less borrowings, so Rs 46,192 cr of disclosed cash contributes nothing to the answer, and the Rs 3,897 cr of trailing other income that cash generates is excluded from the projected cash flows [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.91). For a company where other income is 30.8% of profit before tax [F] (NUMBERS), that is a substantial omission and the model does not size it.

**Its second weakness is the discount rate.** A 15% WACC, built from a 7% risk-free rate, a 7% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.15, is applied to a company with nil debt, an AAA/A1+ rating from two agencies and a sovereign counterparty for 98% of revenue [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.248). [AI] A lower rate is arguable. The sensitivity grid shows that even 13.5% raises the base value only to Rs 1,216.5 [F] (NUMBERS).

**Its third weakness runs the other way.** The model assumes working capital of 153 days against an actual 301 in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS), and assumes a 31% EBITDA margin against HAL's own published operating margin on turnover of 26% [F] (AR2026 p.91). **Both assumptions are generous relative to the latest reported year.**

[AI] **Net assessment: the model is conservative on the balance sheet and generous on operations, and the two do not offset each other in a way that anyone has quantified.** The honest use of it is not as a price target but as a test of what the market is assuming - which is the subject of the next section.

blocks.text: **The key forensic conclusion.** Today's price requires HAL to grow sales at approximately 62.5% a year for five years - roughly nine times its nine-year record, five times management's own FY27 guidance and five times the highest growth rate in our bull case [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Compounded, that implies sales roughly eleven times the current base within five years. **HAL's entire order book of Rs 2,54,538 cr is eight times a single year's turnover and is stated by the company to be executable over seven to eight years** [F] (AR2026 p.35); [MC] (AR2026 p.89). There is no arithmetic path from the disclosed backlog to the required growth rate, and there is no other disclosed source of revenue - no TAM figure, no export book beyond approximately Rs 400 cr, no quantified space or civil-MRO opportunity - that could supply the difference [MC] (CALL May 2026).

The rule-based screen in our statements data reaches the same conclusion and flags it red: 'Price needs growth well above trend. Today's price implies about 62% a year sales growth for five years, against 9% in the base case' [F] (NUMBERS).
[AI] A reverse DCF is only as good as the model it inverts, and this one inherits three specific weaknesses that all push the implied growth requirement upwards.

items: **1. The cash is not in the equity value.** The model defines equity as enterprise value less borrowings, so none of the Rs 46,192 cr of disclosed cash and bank balances is credited [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.91). Equivalently, the enterprise value being solved for is a gross figure that includes the market value of a treasury the cash flows never generate. Any framework that separated the operating business from the treasury would require materially less growth from the operating business than 62.5%.

**2. The other income is not in the cash flows.** Rs 3,897 cr of trailing other income - 30.8% of profit before tax - is excluded from every projected year [F] (NUMBERS). It is real, taxed, cash-generating and has grown every year for five years [F] (AR2026 p.226).

**3. The discount rate is demanding for this risk profile.** 15% on a monopoly supplier to a sovereign counterparty with nil debt, AAA from two agencies, 45-day receivables, nil utilisation of working-capital limits and Rs 73,009 cr of interest-free customer funding [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.284); [F] (NUMBERS).

**4. There is a genuine option that no model captures.** HAL has built capacity for 24-30 fighters and 60 helicopters a year and is currently converting almost none of it into accepted deliveries [MC] (CALL May 2025); [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.251). A monopoly with paid-for idle output capacity, an eight-year backlog and a customer that is also its owner has genuine operating leverage that a growth-rate-and-margin model expresses only crudely.

blocks.text: **Simple average: 4.9 / 10** [E]. **This is not a rating.** [AI] The average conceals the shape, which is what matters: excluding the two valuation factors, the operating and governance average is 5.5 [E]; the business-quality factors alone (revenue visibility, balance sheet, moat, capacity) average 8.0 [E]. **HAL scores as a high-quality, low-growth, badly-governed business at a price that no scenario in the model supports.** The two ones in rows 13 and 14 are doing most of the work in the average, and they are the least debatable entries in the table.

items: **An irreplaceable position.** No second Indian company can integrate and certify a fighter airframe. The barrier is decades of type certification, flight-test infrastructure and an airworthiness relationship, not capital [F] (RATING). The overhaul franchise covering 17+ aircraft types, including platforms HAL did not build, is a multi-decade annuity that recurs independently of new order wins [F] (RATING).

**A balance sheet that cannot fail.** Nil debt, Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank, AAA/A1+ from two agencies, 45-day receivables, nil utilisation of working-capital limits, and Rs 73,009 cr of interest-free customer advances funding the entire working capital [F] (AR2026 p.36, p.91, p.284); [F] (RATING).

**Demand risk is effectively absent.** An order book of Rs 2,54,538 cr, 8.0x turnover, with management expecting a further Rs 90,000 cr over two years and the promoter being the customer [F] (AR2026 p.35); [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Paid-for capacity waiting to be used.** 24-30 fighters and up to 60 helicopters a year of installed capacity, funded from internal accruals, currently converting almost nothing into accepted deliveries [MC] (CALL May 2025); [F] (RATING). If the engine constraint clears, the operating leverage is real and immediate.

**Deferred, not lost.** Thirty-five LCA Mk1A remain contractually due, the airframes are built and engine-ground-run, and 19 are expected by March 2027 [F] (AR2026 p.251); [MC] (CALL May 2026). Roughly Rs 8,000 cr of LCA inventory is waiting to become revenue.

**The price requires the impossible.** The reverse DCF implies approximately 62.5% annual sales growth for five years against a nine-year record of 7.0% [F] (NUMBERS). No cell in the sensitivity grid, and no scenario in the model, produces a value above Rs 1,317.4 against a price of Rs 4,905 [F] (NUMBERS).

**Four consecutive years of missed delivery guidance.** Three aircraft promised for FY24, sixteen for FY25, twelve for FY26, twenty for FY27. Zero signalled out across the first three [MC] (CALL May 2023-2026); [F] (AR2026 p.251).

**Reported profit growth came from provisions and interest, not from operations.** PBT rose Rs 1,292 cr while the provisions charge fell Rs 1,225 cr and other income rose Rs 1,138 cr [F] (AR2026 p.182, p.226). Other income is 30.8% of PBT, the highest in ten years [F] (NUMBERS).

**The annuity has stopped compounding.** ROH services grew 1.6% and spares fell 13.1% in FY26, because - on management's own account - no new platform has been added to the overhaul base [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.226-227); [MC] (CALL May 2026). The delivery failure is now feeding forward into the services business with a three-year lag.

**Cash flow is order-inflow, not profit conversion.** Rs 10,906 cr of CFO required a Rs 20,341 cr increase in liabilities against Rs 18,143 cr absorbed by working capital [F] (AR2026 p.324). The FY17-FY19 precedent shows what the reverse looks like: three years of negative operating cash flow and Rs 5,927 cr of borrowings [F] (NUMBERS).

**Governance is not merely weak; it is formally non-compliant and has been fined.** Zero independent directors for part of FY26, five of seven seats vacant at year end, an auditor Emphasis of Matter, exchange fines, a waiver refused, and an independent director resigning after eleven months disclosed in a footnote [F] (AR2026 p.95, p.108-109, p.157, p.280).

**A monopoly that cannot price.** Cost-plus PPRC pricing, escalation and forex reimbursed at actual, and three years of prices still unsettled with FY26 booked at FY25 rates with no escalation [MC] (CALL May 2026); [F] (RATING); [F] (AR2026 p.250).

subsections.title: What the market may be missing, in both directions

items: **Missed on the bull side: the treasury is worth something and the model gives it nothing.** Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank balances, generating Rs 3,087 cr of interest income, is excluded from the DCF's equity value and from its projected cash flows entirely [F] (AR2026 p.91, p.226); [F] (NUMBERS). Any investor using the -79.3% base-case figure without understanding that omission is using a number that is wrong in a known direction.
**Missed on the bull side: a GE penalty recovery is an unrecognised asset.** Contractual penalty terms exist and management declined to quantify them; nothing is recognised [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Missed on the bull side: FY26 employee costs carried approximately Rs 532 cr of disclosed one-offs** that the company itself says make the year 'not comparable' [F] (AR2026 p.156-157). Normalised operating profit is better than reported.

**Missed on the bear side: the order book is a ceiling, not a floor.** Executed over HAL's own stated 7-8 year horizon, Rs 2,54,538 cr implies Rs 31,817-36,363 cr of annual revenue against FY26 turnover of Rs 31,792 cr [E]. Growth beyond that requires replenishment, which requires the defence budget - which no document in this folder quantifies.

**Missed on the bear side: the successful outcome is margin-dilutive.** Management's target mix of 50:50 moves revenue towards the half it concedes is less profitable, while guiding an unchanged 30-31% margin [MC] (CALL May 2026). Nobody has reconciled those two statements.

**Missed on both sides: value added has fallen from 56.7% to 41.5% of value of production in two years** [E] from [F] (AR2026 p.23-24). This is the clearest quantitative signal in the accounts and it appears in no commentary in the evidence base - not in the calls, not in the MD&A narrative, not in the rating.

items: **The delivery-ramp path.** Engines flow from August 2026, 20 LCA and 20+ HTT-40 are accepted in FY27, LCH production starts FY28 at approximately 30 a year, the 143-ALH contract lands, and by FY31 sales approach the bull-case Rs 61,677 cr at a 33% margin [F] (NUMBERS); [MC] (CALL May 2026). The overhaul base expands as delivered platforms enter their overhaul cycle around FY30. Working capital unwinds, the float shrinks, and other income falls as a share of profit even as operating profit rises. **This is the path management is describing and it produces a fair value of Rs 1,265.1** [F] (NUMBERS).

**The grinding path.** Engines arrive but certification and integration continue to consume time; deliveries run at half the guided rate; revenue compounds at 6-8%; the overhaul annuity grows at 2-4%; margin drifts towards 27-28% as mix shifts; inventory stays above Rs 30,000 cr; and the order book funds the cash flow indefinitely because the Government keeps contracting faster than HAL delivers. [AI] This is the path that the last four years describe and it sits between the bear and base cases.

**The reversal path.** A further engine slip or a fleet grounding, coupled with a year of low order inflow, causes advances to be consumed faster than replenished. Operating cash flow falls sharply, working capital has to be financed, and the company that has had nil debt for five years borrows again - as it did in FY19-FY20 at Rs 5,927 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Reported profit holds up on other income and write-backs, masking the operating deterioration for a year or two.

**The policy path, in both directions.** Upside: the Su-30 upgrade production order of approximately Rs 60,000 cr lands from the sixth year, HAL secures the AMCA production role, and the UH-M and 175-LUH programmes convert [MC] (CALL May 2025); [MC] (CALL May 2023). Downside: procurement migrates from nomination to competitive tender - a threat HAL names itself - and the private-sector supply chain HAL has spent a decade training becomes a bidder [F] (AR2026 p.89).

**The one path nobody is modelling: the treasury.** Cash and bank balances grew from Rs 38,171 cr to Rs 46,192 cr in FY26 alone [F] (AR2026 p.91). On a Rs 3,000 cr capex plan and a 33% payout, the balance keeps compounding. At some point the Government, as a 71.64% shareholder and a fiscally motivated one, will have a view on that. A special dividend, a buyback, or a further offer for sale are all live possibilities that no document in this folder addresses.

blocks.text: **No rating and no price target is offered in this report.** The research view is as follows.

The share price of Rs 4,905 sits above every fair value our model produces under any combination of assumptions we are permitted to use: Rs 737.2 in the bear case, Rs 1,017.5 in the base case, Rs 1,265.1 in the bull case, and Rs 1,317.4 in the most favourable cell of a nine-cell sensitivity grid spanning a 300 basis point range of discount rates [F] (NUMBERS). The implied downside is -85.0%, -79.3% and -74.2% respectively [F] (NUMBERS). The reverse DCF puts the required five-year sales growth at approximately 62.5% a year against a delivered nine-year rate of 7.0% [F] (NUMBERS).

**What drives the gap [AI].** Three things, in descending order of size. First, the model values the operating business only and excludes the Rs 46,192 cr of disclosed cash and the Rs 3,897 cr of trailing other income it generates - a known, directional and unquantified understatement [F] (AR2026 p.91); [F] (NUMBERS). Second, the model applies a 15% cost of equity to a nil-debt, AAA-rated monopoly supplier to a sovereign counterparty; the grid shows that a 13.5% rate raises the base value only to Rs 1,216.5 [F] (NUMBERS). Third - and this is the residual that nothing in the evidence base explains - the market is capitalising the order book, the strategic scarcity of a listed Indian defence monopoly, and a sector re-rating, none of which is a disclosed cash flow. **The first two are legitimate criticisms of the model and together they are not large enough to close the gap. The third is not a valuation argument at all; it is a statement about who is buying.**

subsections.title: Investment horizon and when to re-review

items: [AI] **This is a multi-year holding or nothing.** Revenue recognition is lumpy by construction - Q4 FY26 alone was 42% of the year, and the company discloses that certification and acceptance cluster in the second half on weather grounds [F] (NUMBERS); [F] (AR2026 p.248). A quarter tells you almost nothing. The programme cycles that determine the outcome - LCA Mk1A to FY32-33, LCH over 5.5-6 years, Su-30 upgrade production from the sixth year - run longer than the tenure of any CMD in the record [MC] (CALL May 2024); [MC] (CALL May 2025).

**Re-review trigger 1 - the first Signalling Out Certificate.** Any disclosure that LCA Mk1A deliveries have commenced. This is the single event that converts the entire thesis from potential to actual, and management targeted August-September 2026 [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Re-review trigger 2 - H1 FY27 results (expected around November 2026).** Specifically: manufacturing revenue, inventory and work-in-progress, the provisions charge, other income as a share of PBT, and whether operating cash flow is still liability-funded.

**Re-review trigger 3 - FY27 full-year results and the May 2027 earnings call.** The only management commentary event of the year. Test the 10-12% revenue guidance, the 30-31% margin guidance, the LCA delivery count against approximately 20, the HTT-40 count against '20 plus', and the Rs 90,000 cr two-year order aspiration [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Re-review trigger 4 - the FY27 annual report.** Specifically Note 49 clause 31E (LCA SOC status and LD provision), clause 31C (whether the 4th PPRC has concluded and at what prices), clause 5 (imported share of consumption), clause 49 (provisions movement and write-backs into revenue), clause 52 (gross defence advances), and the Corporate Governance Report on board composition.

**Re-review trigger 5 - any CARE or ICRA rating action.** The negative triggers are explicit: a significant fall in the order book, dilution of Government stake below majority, total debt to PBILDT above 0.50x, or a significant decline in surplus liquidity [F] (RATING).
**Re-review trigger 6 - conversion of the 143-ALH Acceptance of Necessity into a contract**, and any announcement on the Su-30 upgrade CCS approval [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS); [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Re-review trigger 7 - board composition.** Appointment of the remaining independent directors including a woman independent director, and withdrawal of the exchange non-compliance notices [F] (AR2026 p.108).

blocks.text: [AI] **The disclosure to demand before the next review.** HAL publishes no segment data, no capacity utilisation, no delivery schedule and no periodic engine-receipt update, and holds one analyst call a year. An investor in this name is structurally under-informed between May prints. Until segment margins or a delivery schedule are disclosed, the two most informative numbers available are the LCA Signalling Out Certificate count in Note 49 and the year-on-year movement in work-in-progress. Everything else is commentary.

**This is initial coverage.** No previous report exists for this company on this dashboard, so there is no prior quarter's numbers, guidance record, risk assessment or thesis to compare against. The guidance tracker in the governance part has therefore been constructed from four years of earnings-call transcripts (May 2023, May 2024, May 2025 and May 2026) tested against the audited outcomes in the FY26 annual report and the statements data, rather than against a prior report of our own [F] (CALL May 2023-2026); [F] (AR2026); [F] (NUMBERS).

For the avoidance of doubt about the vintage of the evidence: the latest audited accounts are for the year ended 31 March 2026, signed 14 May 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.183); the latest management commentary is the Q4 FY26 call of 15 May 2026 [F] (CALL May 2026); the latest credit rating action is 9 March 2026 [F] (RATING); the latest quarter of financial data is June 2026, the first quarter of FY27, for which **no management commentary exists in the evidence base** [F] (NUMBERS); and the latest exchange announcements run to 10 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). A prospectus or offer document, which would normally provide pre-listing corporate history, was not available.

From the next review onwards, the items to carry forward are the seven re-review triggers set out in the research view, the fifteen guidance items in the guidance tracker, and the thirteen metrics in the monitoring dashboard.

summary.one_line: HAL is a certified monopoly overhaul annuity attached to a Rs 46,192 cr customer-funded treasury, wrapped around a new-build programme that has delivered none of the 35 fighters contractually due across three years - and its share price of Rs 4,905 implies about 62.5% annual sales growth for five years against a nine-year record of 7.0%, a gap that no scenario, discount rate or sensitivity cell in our model can bridge.

[F] (AR2026 p.284) The customer pre-funds the entire business: gross advances from defence customers rose Rs 21,721 cr to Rs 73,009 cr in FY26, they are interest-free [F] (RATING), and they underwrite nil borrowings, Rs 46,192 cr of cash and bank balances [F] (AR2026 p.91), AAA/A1+ ratings from two agencies and nil utilisation of Rs 4,000 cr of working-capital limits.

[F] (AR2026 p.35) Demand risk is effectively absent: the order book stands at Rs 2,54,538 cr, 8.0x FY26 turnover [E], after fresh orders of Rs 97,028 cr in FY26 and Rs 1,25,280 cr in FY25 [MC] (CALL May 2026); [MC] (CALL May 2025), with management expecting a further Rs 90,000 cr over two years.
